name: Yara Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: History and politics, so a lot of reading. Two lectures a day, a seminar where I'm still working up the nerve to disagree with people, and the rest in the library. I shelve books at the public library on Thursday evenings and Sunday afternoons. I share a room in student housing with a girl called Mei who's studying chemistry. My mum works for the council planning office and my dad teaches geography, so I grew up with a lot of dinner-table arguments about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief and also a bit funny, since history is full of technology that was going to change everything and mostly changed a little. I'd mention the printing press and the telegraph, and then admit that sometimes the hype was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, calm. I want to teach or work in the civil service, and both of those are slow-moving. My mum says the council still prints things out for committees. I do use an AI tool to summarise long readings sometimes, and it's helpful, but it gets names wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Keep my shifts at the library, do the readings myself and use the tool only as a second check. I'd try to save about 30 a month, and think about doing a teaching placement in second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Even a bit pleased. A degree in history is easier to enjoy when nobody's telling you it's worthless. The only bit that sits on me is the loan, and the fact that Dad paid for my first term deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tool gets names wrong. How do you check it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I go back to the page. I've had it tell me the wrong king for a battle, with total confidence. So I only trust it as a pointer, not an answer. It's a bit like a classmate who's keen but unreliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that say about how you'd treat any new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd test it on something I already know. If a tool gets my subject wrong, I'm not going to trust it on a subject I don't know. I think that's sensible, but my friends say I'm slow to commit, and they might be right.

say: I'd say **history** is full of technology that changed less than promised.
I'd admit the hype was **sometimes right**.
think: Teaching and the civil service are **slow-moving**, so I feel calm.
The **loan** is the thing that actually sits on me.
do: **Keep** the library shifts and do the readings myself.
**Use** the AI tool only as a second check.
**Save** 30 a month and look into a teaching placement.
feel: **Okay**, even a bit pleased that history isn't called worthless.
A quiet **weight** from the loan and my dad's help.
S0.quote: If a tool gets my subject wrong, I'm not going to trust it on a subject I don't know.
fieldNote: Her **historian's habit** of checking sources shapes how she uses AI.
Calm because her target jobs, teaching and civil service, move slowly.
Quietly aware of the debt and her father's help.

steps.text: Keep shelving books at the library on Thursdays and Sundays
Save 30 a month from library pay
Use the AI tool only to double-check my reading notes
Ask about a teaching placement in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been here before, with the weavers and the clerks, and the question isn't whether jobs change but who gets looked after when they do. I'd bring it up in my politics seminar, because I think the interesting part is the policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, uneasy. A lot of what a civil service entry job involves is drafting letters, summarising reports and answering queries, and that's the stuff described on the card. Teaching feels safer, but even there, marking and lesson planning would shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tool, but more carefully, and learn what it's good at. I'd take a data and statistics module, because government will want people who can question the machine's output. And I'd ask my mum which jobs in her office have been cut or not replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thoughtful rather than scared. A bit like reading about a revolution while living through the start of one. I'd be curious, and there'd be a small cold patch of worry about where I'd fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said who gets looked after when jobs change. Who do you mean, and who should look after them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who do routine clerical work and are midway through their careers, like the women in my mum's office who've been there twenty years. I think government and employers share the job: retraining that's paid for, not just a leaflet. I'm in the middle on most things, but I don't think the market sorts this out alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your mum tell you about her office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they've frozen two admin posts and moved to a system that sorts planning applications. Nobody was sacked, they just didn't replace people when they left. The pattern I'd expect is quiet shrinking, with nobody sacked, just posts left empty when people leave. Not a headline.

say: I'd say we've been here before, and **who gets looked after** is the question.
I'd raise it in my **politics seminar**.
think: Entry-level **civil service work** is drafting and summarising, the work software takes.
Teaching feels safer, but **marking and planning** would shift.
do: **Learn** what the AI tool is actually good at.
**Ask** my mum which office jobs went unfilled.
feel: **Thoughtful** rather than scared, like watching history begin.
A small **cold patch** about where I'd fit.
S1.quote: The pattern I'd expect is quiet shrinking, with nobody sacked, just posts left empty when people leave.
fieldNote: Uses **history** and her mum's office as evidence, not headlines.
Names the pattern as quiet shrinking, which is exactly what the card implies.
Centre politics: wants shared responsibility between government and employers.

steps.text: Take a statistics module to question machine output
Test the AI tool on topics I already know well
Ask Mum which council posts went unfilled
Join the student politics society's policy group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years isn't enough for any government I've read about. States take a decade to change a tax form. I'd say that firmly and then feel foolish because nobody would be listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened. Everything I'm training for, writing, reading, arguing, is thinking work. If AI does that as well and cheaper, a history degree is a piece of paper, and the civil service might simply shrink. I'd also think about my parents' jobs, since a planner and a teacher are both exposed in different ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, because it's the only structure I have, but I'd look at how I could get something hands-on or relational, like a nursing or social care route, or becoming a teacher in a hands-on subject. I'd ask my dad whether he'd retire early. And I'd save everything from the library job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the end of an exam when you realise you've misread the question. A sort of hot embarrassment, and then fear. I'd call Mei, my flatmate, and we'd probably stay up till two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask your dad about retiring early. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's 55, and the school's already talked about computer-led lessons. If he's going to be pushed out, I'd rather it was on his terms, with the pension he's earned. I'd also want him around, honestly. I'd like to have a long talk with him about what he'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the history degree stopped making sense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the year and then look at a course that leads to a job where a person has to be in the room. I'd think about a care route, or occupational therapy. I'd feel I'd wasted a year, but my dad says nothing you learn is wasted, which is easy to say when you're 55 and secure.

say: I'd say **two years** isn't enough for any government I've read about.
I'd feel foolish saying it into **silence**.
think: Writing and arguing are **thinking work**, so my degree could be worth little.
My parents' jobs, a planner and a teacher, are both **exposed**.
do: **Keep** studying because it's my only structure.
**Look** at nursing or social care routes.
**Ask** my dad about retiring early on his terms.
feel: **Hot embarrassment** then fear, like misreading an exam question.
**Comforted** by staying up late with my flatmate Mei.
S2.quote: I'd finish the year and then look at a course that leads to a job where a person has to be in the room.
fieldNote: Her worry is both **personal and parental**, as both parents' jobs are exposed.
Plans a pivot to **hands-on** work while finishing the year first.
Her father's reassurance helps but she notes he is secure.

steps.text: Keep studying while researching nursing and social care routes
Talk to Dad about retiring early on his own terms
Save every pound from the library job
Finish the year before deciding whether to switch course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if people are honest about it. I'd push for my university to be clear about what its graduates will do. I'd also write an essay on it, because writing helps me think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'd graduate in 2029 into the middle of it. That's tricky, but not hopeless. I'd have time to get a teaching qualification or a master's, and teaching still needs a person in the room, at least for children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for a postgraduate teaching qualification, since that's a path where a human is the point. I'd do a placement in a school in second year, volunteer at the library's homework club, and save about 50 a month. And I'd get better with the tools, because teachers will have to use them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with a thin wire of anxiety. Five years feels like an assignment with a deadline. I do those fairly well, but not without a bad night or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a teacher is a person in the room. Do you think that holds through 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For older students, who might learn from a tutor tool at home, I'm less sure. For young children, parents want a human in the room, so I would aim at primary school where the job is half care and half teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would you do about the debt in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep it small, and avoid a second degree if I can. A teaching qualification is one year, and I'd earn a wage while I do it. If it went wrong I'd move back with my parents for a while, which isn't a disaster, just not what I planned.

say: I'd say five years is long enough **if people are honest**.
I'd write an **essay** on it, because writing helps me think.
think: I'd graduate in **2029** into the middle of the change.
Teaching still needs **a person** in the room, at least for young children.
do: **Do** a school placement and volunteer at a homework club.
**Save** 50 a month and learn the tools teachers will use.
feel: **Steady**, with a thin wire of anxiety.
S3.quote: For young children, parents want a human in the room, so I would aim at primary school where the job is half care and half teaching.
fieldNote: Reasons about **which teaching jobs** keep a human at the centre.
Fallback is modest: moving back to her parents' house.
Treats the future like an assignment, which suits her temperament.

steps.text: Apply for a school placement in second year
Plan a one-year postgraduate teaching course
Save 50 a month from library pay
Learn the lesson-planning tools teachers will be expected to use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance to get it right, and if we mess it up we can't say we weren't warned. I'd say governments should start writing the rules now. I'd say it with my history hat on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, quite calm. I'd be 28, with a qualification and some experience. The robots wouldn't come for another three years after that. I'd have time to try teaching and see whether it holds, and to change if it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do a teaching or civil service route, and stay curious about the tools. I'd keep saving, about 100 a month once I'm earning. And I'd keep studying history, because someone has to explain how we got here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Like having a long reading list and the whole term to do it. Not nothing, but not a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a decade to buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A chance to try. If I teach for five years and the job starts to change, I'd still have time to move into training or policy. A decade means one wrong turn doesn't ruin everything. In the faster pictures, every choice feels like the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something you'd worry about even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people won't use the time. History says we wait until it's a crisis. Having ten years is only useful if people act in year two, not year nine. I don't have a lot of faith in that.

say: I'd say ten years is a chance to **get it right**.
I'd say governments should start writing the **rules** now.
think: At 28 I'd have a **qualification** and experience, and three years before robots.
Ten years means one **wrong turn** doesn't ruin everything.
do: **Finish** the degree and train as a teacher or civil servant.
**Keep** studying history in my own time.
feel: **Settled**, like a long reading list and a whole term.
S4.quote: Having ten years is only useful if people act in year two, not year nine.
fieldNote: Time gives her room for **mistakes**, which she says the faster worlds don't.
Her one fear is human: that people will wait for a crisis.
Calm is based on a clear plan and a family safety net.

steps.text: Finish the degree and apply for teacher training
Put 100 a month aside once I'm in work
Vote and write to my MP about preparing early
Spend more time with my parents while Dad's still teaching

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years gives a government no time to respond and gives me no time to adapt, and both my parents work in jobs that would be hit. What would help is honest information early, and the state being ready with retraining and some form of income for people caught out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that people my age are quieter about this than it looks, because we're all pretending to be relaxed. Everyone else seems to be. I think a few honest conversations would help more than a lot of reports.

headlineQuote: People my age are quieter about this than it looks, because we're all pretending to be relaxed.
portrait: Yara is an **18-year-old** history and politics student who shelves library books and reads everything twice.
She uses AI **now and then**, but checks it against the page after it named the wrong king.
Her **centre** view is that markets alone won't look after people, so government and employers should share it.
Both parents are **exposed**: a council planner and a geography teacher, and she knows it.
She moves from calm in the quiet world to anxious at 2028, then settled again when ten years leaves room for mistakes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both parents' jobs and her own path would be hit with no time.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **early information** and ready-made retraining and income support.
More **open conversations** among young people, who are quiet about their worry.
